doc.title: Chuck Mancuso interviewed by Monk Rowe, Buffalo, New York, October 10, 2013

title: Sicilian family and clothier uncles
summary: He describes his Sicilian and central Italian relatives, uncles who were clothiers and salesmen, and how they taught him to dress sharp.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Where I came from: parents, siblings and birth

blocks.x: Yes. And that’s after they kind of gave up a little bit on jazz, but there had to be something there that kept them with it. So here I was in school, and we were a nomadic tribe. We moved. It was like the Italians — and we weren’t alone with the Italians — but my father’s family, they were Sicilian, the Mancusos. And his father, and they had four kids, three boys and a girl. And they bought a house. You know, they were from Sicily. And they made sure that there was room for the sons. Okay? And as the sons got married there was a place. My mother’s people were from the middle of Italy, and he was a hard working guy. You know, he used to say, “Marie, you do not date those Sicilian boys, do they not like to get their fingers dirty, their fingernails dirty.” And it’s true. They were slickers. The Sicilians were slickers. There were a lot of stones, you know, everybody kind of dominated, and that’s where the mob kind of stuff came from. And all of those guys went into sales. They were slick guys you know. My uncle Bay, he was always a baker, and they at Kresberries, and then a buyer at Sattlers and he used to call me up, “Nef, I just got back from a slack bar, and I got a great tiger-tooth two button, and I can get you a nice pair of creased, you know with our tailor, come on down and we’ll take care of it. I always just put a little money down and I always did a little extra work. And my uncle Blase, who I was with last night, he worked at A M & A’s. These guys were all clothiers. And he’d go, “Chuckie, you’ve got to understand, “You know, Uncle Blase, “You’ve got to understand it doesn’t matter about the first suit you sell. Anybody can sell the suit. You treat ‘em nice, they come back again.” That’s the way he talked, I’m telling you. It was unbelievable.
So I knew how to dress man. I dressed all the time.
Always sharp. Yeah. Because of them. And Uncle Bay was pretty slick. He’d go, “You ain’t no Cary Grant but you sure will be able to dress well.”
